_what: The Planet Nine debate (search/timeline.html, charts/debate.js): one dot per paper in papers.json from 2014 on, for a planet inside the circle, against outside, revealed year by year.
_caution: Which side a paper is on comes from 'stance' in papers.json, our editorial reading of its abstract: supports -> for; against and alternative -> against; neutral (data, models, predictions that take no side) is left out of the picture but stays in papers.json and on the credits page.
A paper's year is its year in field_timeline.json when the ledger has it, otherwise its year in papers.json.

'why' is the one line that says what a paper does to the argument. For papers in field_timeline.json it is that file's line (the branch's title when the finders drew a conclusion, else the entry's title); the lines below are for the rest, each a retelling of the abstract-checked 'summary' in papers.json. Tagged ours.
'headlines' are ours: one line per year, naming only papers in the picture that year (and Rubin's start in 2026, from field_timeline.json). They are a reading, not a finding.
The sample is chosen, not a census; counting its dots does not measure opinion.

headlines.2014: A second remote orbit hints at a hidden planet, while an infrared survey finds no large one nearby
headlines.2015: No paper in this sample. The two remote orbits remain the main clue
headlines.2016: Batygin and Brown propose Planet Nine, and others find routes to the same planet
headlines.2017: First doubts: the alignment may come from where telescopes happened to look
headlines.2018: A steeply tilted orbit fits the planet, and a first explanation without one appears
headlines.2019: Brown and Batygin put the odds of chance at 1 in 500; a disk of small bodies is offered instead
headlines.2020: More alternatives: bodies that line themselves up, or a black hole in the planet's place
headlines.2021: A refined orbit for the planet, and three surveys that see no significant clustering
headlines.2022: The first direct search rules out half of the predicted planets
headlines.2023: Modified gravity is offered as another way to line up the orbits
headlines.2024: Three-quarters of the predicted planets are ruled out, and a passing star is offered instead
headlines.2025: A possible infrared sighting, and two remote objects whose orbits do not fit the pattern
headlines.2026: No paper in this sample yet. The Rubin survey, the likeliest to settle the question, begins

why.10.3847/2041-8205/824/2/L23: Shows where surveys have already looked along the predicted orbit, and where the planet could still be.
why.10.3847/1538-3881/153/3/91: Fits an orbit for the planet by asking it to share simple rhythms with the known extreme objects.
why.10.1016/j.physrep.2019.01.009: Gathers the evidence and revises the planet to 5 to 10 Earth masses, 400 to 800 AU out.
why.10.3847/1538-3881/aaf0fc: A massive disk of small bodies could line the orbits up with no planet.
why.10.3847/2041-8213/ab91a0: The distant bodies' own pull can produce the same alignment, mimicking the planet's signal.
why.10.1103/PhysRevLett.125.051103: Keeps the mass and the orbit, but puts a grapefruit-sized black hole where the planet would be.
why.10.3847/1538-4365/ac3914: A survey that tracks its own blind spots finds its extreme objects spread evenly, not lined up.
why.10.3847/1538-3881/acef1e: Modified gravity could line up the orbits with no ninth planet.
why.10.1038/s41550-024-02349-x: A star passing close to the young Sun could have shaped the distant orbits instead.
